claims.claim: The wild-type recombination rate (9.9% recombination-positive colonies) increased when both difH sites were replaced with difHLP (29.4%; p=0.0016, t-test), but decreased to barely detectable levels with difHRP (1.3%; p=0.0021, t-test).
claims.source: An assay that assesses the efficiency of intramolecular recombination between two plasmid-borne sites in E. coli also indicated differential activity at the two difH arms in vivo: the wild-type recombination rate (9.9% recombination-positive colonies) increased when both difH sites were replaced with difHLP (29.4%; p=0.0016, t-test), but decreased to barely detectable levels with difHRP (1.3%; p=0.0021, t-test) (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo recombination assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The sequences of the two arms are identical apart from a single base-pair insertion in the left arm.
claims.source: Remarkably, the sequences of the two arms are identical apart from a single base-pair insertion in the left arm (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the sequence shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The inserted base-pair (A6/T25', brown in Figure 2A) is not recognized directly.
claims.source: The inserted base-pair (A6/T25', brown in Figure 2A) is not recognized directly.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claims.claim: In the left arm, T4 forms hydrophobic contacts with XerH αK and makes a specific hydrogen bond with lysine K290, whereas in the right arm T5' is closer to the center of difH and cannot make these interactions.
claims.source: Instead, the main difference in the recognition of the two arms involves a conserved thymine base (T4/T5') in the outer parts of the arms: In the left arm, T4 forms hydrophobic contacts with XerH αK and makes a specific hydrogen bond with lysine K290 (Figure 3F, red insert), whereas in the right arm T5' is closer to the center of difH and cannot make these interactions.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The three outermost base-pairs of each difH arm make very similar backbone interactions with their respective XerH subunits, despite the fact that they are shifted in space due to the insertion in the left arm.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the three outermost base-pairs of each difH arm make very similar backbone interactions with their respective XerH subunits, despite the fact that they are shifted in space due to the insertion in the left arm (altering the 'helical phase' of the sequence by ~35°; Figure 3F, black insert; Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: The conformation of the DNA is asymmetric – the left arm is more bent than the right arm – and the catalytic domains of the protein subunits are rotated by ~10° relative to each other.
claims.source: This is possible because the conformation of the DNA is asymmetric – the left arm is more bent than the right arm – and the catalytic domains of the protein subunits are rotated by ~10° relative to each other (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The observed differences result in stronger interaction of XerH with the left difH arm (ΔG = −21.3 kcal/mol) than with the right arm (ΔG = −15.4 kcal/mol).
claims.source: Together, the observed differences result in stronger interaction of XerH with the left difH arm (ΔG = −21.3 kcal/mol, estimated by PISA [Krissinel and Henrick, 2007]) than with the right arm (ΔG = −15.4 kcal/mol).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure using PISA.

claims.claim: While the αN-αO segment of molecule A is fully ordered, the linker and αO are partially disordered in molecule B.
claims.source: A further difference between the XerH subunits bound to the left and right arms of difH concerns the C-terminal helices. While the αN-αO segment of molecule A is fully ordered, the linker and αO are partially disordered in molecule B.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claims.claim: Helices αO point in different directions (~100° rotation).
claims.source: Also, helices αO point in different directions (~100° rotation; Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: difH variants containing mutations at the inserted base-pair showed no or only moderate decreases in cleavage in vitro and recombination in vivo.
claims.source: In agreement with the structure, difH variants containing mutations at the inserted base-pair showed no or only moderate decreases in cleavage in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) and recombination in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cleavage and recombination assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: Substitutions of T4 practically abolished recombination in E. coli and in H. pylori.
claims.source: In contrast, substitutions of T4 practically abolished recombination in E. coli (Figure 3E) and in H. pylori (Debowski et al., 2012a); and mutation of K290 (K290S) decreased recombination activity by about half (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by recombination assay data shown in Figure 3E and cited data from Debowski et al., 2012a.

claims.claim: Mutation of K290 (K290S) decreased recombination activity by about half.
claims.source: In contrast, substitutions of T4 practically abolished recombination in E. coli (Figure 3E) and in H. pylori (Debowski et al., 2012a); and mutation of K290 (K290S) decreased recombination activity by about half (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by recombination assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: Insertion of an additional base-pair next to A6/T25' in the left arm abolished cleavage completely.
claims.source: Insertion of an additional base-pair next to A6/T25' in the left arm, further shifting the positions of the three outermost base-pairs, also abolished cleavage completely (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: XerH does not contact the nucleotides flanking the left and right cleavage sites (positions C13 and G13').
claims.source: However, XerH does not contact these nucleotides in our structure, and cleavage assays with difH variants carrying mutations at these positions revealed no reduction in activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), suggesting that the identity of these nucleotides does not contribute to XerH binding and cleavage asymmetry.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: XerH binds preferentially to the left arm of difH thanks to favorable interactions with its outer sequence (including T4).
claims.source: Together, these data demonstrate that XerH binds preferentially to the left arm of difH thanks to favorable interactions with its outer sequence (including T4).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data presented.

claims.claim: Asymmetric interactions with the two arms of difH dictate distinct protein conformations in the synaptic complex, including differential positioning of the αN-αO segment that carries the nucleophilic tyrosine, perhaps helping to define which arm is cleaved first.
claims.source: Asymmetric interactions with the two arms of difH also appear to dictate distinct protein conformations in the synaptic complex, including differential positioning of the αN-αO segment that carries the nucleophilic tyrosine, perhaps helping to define which arm is cleaved first.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claims.claim: Both DNA molecules in the synapse resemble B-form DNA, with a wide angle (165°) between the two difH arms.
claims.source: Both DNA molecules in the synapse resemble B-form DNA, with a wide angle (165°) between the two difH arms (Figure 2B, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The loxP DNA is bent to ~100° in the analogous pre-cleavage structures of Cre-loxP complexes.
claims.source: For example, the loxP DNA is bent to ~100° in the analogous pre-cleavage structures of Cre-loxP complexes (Figure 2B, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with known structures shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: In the active site of each XerH subunit, several conserved residues including the catalytic tyrosine Y344, two arginine (R213 and R312), and two histidine (H309 and H335) residues are assembled around the scissile phosphate.
claims.source: In the active site of each XerH subunit, several conserved residues including the catalytic tyrosine Y344, two arginine (R213 and R312), and two histidine (H309 and H335) residues are assembled around the scissile phosphate, together forming a catalytic pocket characteristic of tyrosine recombinases.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The active sites of the subunits are very similar, except for the R213 side chain which points in different directions in molecules A and B.
claims.source: The active sites of the subunits are very similar, except for the R213 side chain which points in different directions in molecules A and B (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Electron density for another essential catalytic residue, K239, could not be observed in either of the subunits, so it is presumed to be disordered.
claims.source: Electron density for another essential catalytic residue, K239, could not be observed in either of the subunits, so we presume that it is disordered.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The catalytic tyrosine Y344 is far away (5.2–5.8 Å) from the scissile phosphate in all subunits, so the structure represents a catalytically inactive synaptic complex.
claims.source: The catalytic tyrosine Y344 is far away (5.2–5.8 Å) from the scissile phosphate in all subunits, so the structure represents a catalytically inactive synaptic complex, implying a conformational change is required prior to catalysis.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The post-cleavage structure differs considerably from the pre-cleavage structure.
claims.source: The resulting structure (Figure 4A) differs considerably from the pre-cleavage structure.
claims.evidence: This is a direct comparison between the two structures shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In the post-cleavage structure, the two halves of the tetramer are related by crystallographic two-fold symmetry.
claims.source: Each difHLP site interacts with two XerH molecules in a tetrameric synaptic complex, but in this structure, the two halves of the tetramer are related by crystallographic two-fold symmetry (relating molecule A to A' and B to B'; Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The difH DNA is strongly bent in the post-cleavage structure.
claims.source: Most strikingly, the difH DNA is now strongly bent (Figure 4B, Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4B and Video 1.

claims.claim: The bend mainly originates from a single distortion within the central region of difH: bases A17' and G18' are un-stacked with a 90° tilt, which introduces a kink resulting in asymmetric bending of the DNA.
claims.source: The bend mainly originates from a single distortion within the central region of difH: bases A17' and G18' are un-stacked with a 90° tilt, which introduces a kink resulting in asymmetric bending of the DNA (insert in Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The total angle of 120° between the difH arms is only slightly wider than the angles observed in previous structures of various tyrosine recombinases.
claims.source: The total angle of 120° between the difH arms is only slightly wider than the angles observed in previous structures of various tyrosine recombinases (e.g. 109° in the post-cleavage structure of λ integrase (Biswas et al., 2005) and 100° in Cre-loxP (Guo et al., 1997); see also Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a direct comparison with cited structures.

claims.claim: The kink in difH is at an equivalent position to the kink in loxP.
claims.source: Notably, the kink in difH is at an equivalent position to the kink in loxP (Ennifar et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with cited structures.

claims.claim: In Cre, the nucleotides involved in the kink interact with three arginines within a tight pocket, whereas XerH forms only a single interaction with these nucleotides (R129-A17') and encircles the kink less tightly.
claims.source: However, whereas in Cre the nucleotides involved in the kink interact with three arginines within a tight pocket (Figure 4C) (Ennifar et al., 2003; Guo et al., 1997), XerH forms only a single interaction with these nucleotides (R129-A17'; Figure 4C; Figure 2—figure supplement 4A) and encircles the kink less tightly.
claims.evidence: This is a direct comparison between the XerH structure and cited Cre structures shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The nucleotides of the central region of difH remain fully base-paired after cleavage, unlike the analogous structure of Cre-loxP, where several of these are unpaired.
claims.source: Notably, the nucleotides of the central region of difH remain fully base-paired after cleavage, unlike the analogous structure of Cre-loxP, where several of these are unpaired (Guo et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is a direct comparison with cited Cre-loxP structures.

claims.claim: Extensive Cre contacts can actively bend loxP, whereas weaker XerH-difH interactions appear to be insufficient to promote sharp DNA bending.
claims.source: The extensive Cre contacts can thus actively bend loxP. In contrast, weaker XerH-difH interactions appear to be insufficient to promote sharp DNA bending, but nicks in both DNA strands of the difH substrate facilitate bending.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison and the observation that nicked substrates were used.

claims.claim: Nicks in both DNA strands of the difH substrate facilitate bending.
claims.source: The extensive Cre contacts can thus actively bend loxP. In contrast, weaker XerH-difH interactions appear to be insufficient to promote sharp DNA bending, but nicks in both DNA strands of the difH substrate facilitate bending.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and the use of nicked substrates.

claims.claim: When the DNA strands in the post-cleavage structure were re-built to model a bent but un-nicked substrate, a clash with the protein near the tyrosine nucleophile-bearing helix αN was observed, suggesting that the nicks might favor the XerH conformation adopted on the bent sites.
claims.source: When we tried to re-build the DNA strands in the post-cleavage structure to model a bent but un-nicked substrate, we observed a clash with the protein near the tyrosine nucleophile-bearing helix αN, suggesting that the nicks might favor the XerH conformation adopted on the bent sites.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on molecular modeling.

claims.claim: Each subunit is rotated by ~22° in the post-cleavage structure, resulting in major rewiring of the inter-subunit interactions and an overall compaction of the complex.
claims.source: The arrangement of the XerH subunits is also markedly different in the two structures. Each subunit is rotated by ~22° in the post-cleavage structure (Figure 4B, Video 1), resulting in major rewiring of the inter-subunit interactions and an overall compaction of the complex.
claims.evidence: This is a direct comparison between the two structures shown in Figure 4B and Video 1.

claims.claim: The synaptic interface is considerably larger (3926 Å2) in the post-cleavage structure than in the pre-cleavage structure (3040 Å2).
claims.source: Also, the synaptic interface is considerably larger (3926 Å2, calculated by PISA [Krissinel and Henrick, 2007]) than in the pre-cleavage structure (3040 Å2).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structures using PISA.

claims.claim: The previously disordered parts of the αO helices of molecule B are now fully visible, ordered, and more compact in the post-cleavage structure.
claims.source: The previously disordered parts of the αO helices of molecule B are now fully visible, ordered, and more compact (F338 - W359 distance reduced from 43 Å to 34 Å; Figure 4D, left insert).
claims.evidence: This is a direct comparison between the two structures shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Helices αN and αO of molecule A are rotated by ~30° in the post-cleavage structure, bringing the catalytic Y344 to a suitable position to attack one strand on each difHLP DNA forming a covalent phosphotyrosyl bond.
claims.source: At the same time, helices αN and αO of molecule A are rotated by ~30°, bringing the catalytic Y344 to a suitable position to attack one strand on each difHLP DNA forming a covalent phosphotyrosyl bond (Figure 4E, left).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Despite the symmetry of the palindromic difHLP substrate, the two bound XerH molecules (A and B) are in different conformations.
claims.source: Interestingly, despite the symmetry of the palindromic difHLP substrate, the two bound XerH molecules (A and B) are in different conformations (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Subunit A assumes a fully active conformation, while subunit B is in an inactive conformation with the catalytic tyrosine distant from the scissile phosphate.
claims.source: Consequently, subunit A assumes a fully active conformation, while subunit B is in an inactive conformation with the catalytic tyrosine distant from the scissile phosphate (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The simultaneous presence of both active and inactive XerH subunit conformations within the synaptic complex is consistent with the 'half-of-the-sites reactivity' mechanism observed for other tyrosine recombinases.
claims.source: This simultaneous presence of both active and inactive XerH subunit conformations within the synaptic complex is consistent with the 'half-of-the-sites reactivity' mechanism observed for other tyrosine recombinases (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and comparison with known mechanisms.

claims.claim: The marked difference between the XerH subunits bound to the two difHLP arms is particularly striking considering that the artificially introduced symmetry of the substrate could be expected to mask some asymmetric features of the synaptic complex.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claims.claim: The asymmetry is presumably an intrinsic property of the system, essential to the mechanism of synapsis and catalysis.
claims.source: The asymmetry is presumably an intrinsic property of the system, essential to the mechanism of synapsis and catalysis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claims.claim: Due to high structural conservation within the Xer family, the XerH structures can provide insights into the mechanisms of other Xer recombinases.
claims.source: Due to high structural conservation within the Xer family (Subramanya et al., 1997) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), our XerH structures can provide insights into the mechanisms of other Xer recombinases that have eluded structural studies so far.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and cited structural data.

claims.claim: The models place XerC on the right arm of difH and XerD on the left arm.
claims.source: Our models place XerC on the right arm of difH and XerD on the left arm.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the modeling approach.

claims.claim: The observation that XerH preferentially cleaves at the left arm of difH first supports the hypothesis that the XerH subunit on the left arm corresponds to XerD whereas the subunit on the right arm corresponds to XerC.
claims.source: We cannot exclude the alternative assignment, but our observation that XerH preferentially cleaves at the left arm of difH first (Figure 3D) supports the hypothesis that the XerH subunit on the left arm corresponds to XerD whereas the subunit on the right arm corresponds to XerC.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cleavage data shown in Figure 3D and analogy with the XerC/D system.

claims.claim: In the models, the XerC and XerD monomers each form C-shaped clamps around one arm of the dif site.
claims.source: In the models, the XerC and XerD monomers each form C-shaped clamps around one arm of the dif site (Figure 5B), and make multiple sequence-specific and backbone interactions with the DNA.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the models shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The five conserved catalytic residues (RHRHY) assemble around the catalytic pocket in all XerC and XerD subunits.
claims.source: The five conserved catalytic residues (RHRHY) assemble around the catalytic pocket in all XerC and XerD subunits (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the models shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: In the post-cleavage complex model, the XerD subunits are in an active conformation, with their nucleophilic tyrosines approaching the scissile phosphates, whereas the XerC subunits are in an inactive conformation.
claims.source: In the post-cleavage complex, the XerD subunits are in an active conformation, with their nucleophilic tyrosines approaching the scissile phosphates, whereas the XerC subunits are in an inactive conformation.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the models.

claims.claim: The three outer base-pairs of each dif arm are contacted extensively by the proteins in the models, and the bases corresponding to T4 in difH interact with lysine K222 of XerC or histidine H225 of XerD.
claims.source: As in the XerH structures, the three outer base-pairs of each dif arm are contacted extensively by the proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), and the bases corresponding to T4 in difH interact with lysine K222 of XerC or histidine H225 of XerD, both counterparts of XerH K290 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the models shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: These interactions might contribute to the arm specificity of XerC and XerD, as well as to ordering recombination.
claims.source: These interactions might contribute to the arm specificity of XerC and XerD, as well as to ordering recombination, as we inferred for XerH.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the models and analogy with XerH.

claims.claim: The interactions involved in DNA kinking in Cre are absent in the XerC/D-dif complex, suggesting that these enzymes, like XerH, might be unable to independently initiate sharp DNA bending.
claims.source: The interactions involved in DNA kinking in Cre are absent in the XerC/D-dif complex, suggesting that these enzymes, like XerH, might be unable to independently initiate sharp DNA bending.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the models and comparison with Cre.

claims.claim: The protein arrangements and interfaces observed in the two XerH-difH structures are well accommodated by XerC and XerD.
claims.source: The protein arrangements and interfaces observed in our two XerH-difH structures are well accommodated by XerC and XerD, the pre-cleavage model showing nearly straight DNA and the post-cleavage model containing bent DNA and tightened intersubunit interactions (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the models shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The XerC/D and XerH complexes might undergo similar conformational rearrangements upon activation.
claims.source: This suggests that the XerC/D and XerH complexes might undergo similar conformational rearrangements upon activation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the models.

claims.claim: Two previous smFRET studies reported that pre-formed XerC/D-dif synaptic complexes undergo conformational change upon activation by FtsK, leading to an increase of the distance between the two dif termini from about 53 to 67 Å across the synapse.
claims.source: In agreement with this idea, two previous smFRET studies (Diagne et al., 2014; Zawadzki et al., 2013) reported that pre-formed XerC/D-dif synaptic complexes undergo conformational change upon activation by FtsK, leading to an increase of the distance between the two dif termini from about 53 to 67 Å across the synapse (as predicted from a change in FRET efficiencies; [Zawadzki et al., 2013]).

claims.claim: The XerC/D-dif models predict a similar change from 46 Å in the pre-cleavage state to 60 Å in the post-cleavage state.
claims.source: Our XerC/D-dif models predict a similar change from 46 Å in the pre-cleavage state to 60 Å in the post-cleavage state.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the models and comparison with smFRET data.

claims.claim: Xer proteins follow the established chemical pathway of tyrosine recombinases.

claims.claim: The reaction steps can be choreographed by small differences in the arms of the difH recombination sites.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data.

claims.claim: XerH-difH synaptic complexes initially assemble in an inactive state with straight DNA, which must undergo a major conformational change for catalytic activation.
claims.source: Together with associated biochemical data, the structures also show that XerH-difH synaptic complexes initially assemble in an inactive state with straight DNA, which must undergo a major conformational change for catalytic activation, as previously observed in single molecule fluorescence studies of XerC/D-dif recombination (Diagne et al., 2014; Zawadzki et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data, supported by citations to smFRET studies.

claims.claim: The post-cleavage XerH-difH synaptic complex structure elucidates the structural nature of the conformational change, which involves major rearrangement of the protein-protein interfaces and DNA bending.
claims.source: Our post-cleavage XerH-difH synaptic complex structure elucidates the structural nature of this conformational change, which involves major rearrangement of the protein-protein interfaces and DNA bending (Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the structural data shown in Video 1.

claims.claim: The structures provide a resource for understanding the mechanism of other Xer recombinases.
claims.source: With molecular modeling, we extend our structural and mechanistic findings to the prototypical E. coli XerC/D-dif system, demonstrating that our structures provide a resource for understanding the mechanism of other Xer recombinases.

claims.claim: The recombination process starts with XerH binding to the difH site on the H. pylori chromosome.
claims.source: The recombination process starts with XerH binding to the difH site on the H. pylori chromosome (Figure 6A).

claims.claim: Two XerH subunits bind cooperatively to one difH site.
claims.source: Two XerH subunits bind cooperatively to one difH site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 6A), each forming a clamp around one arm of difH (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and structural data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The difH left arm has higher affinity for XerH than the right arm, leading to the second XerH molecule binding to the right arm more often than vice versa.

results.result: The pre-cleavage XerH-difH synaptic complex structure reveals a tetrameric assembly with two difH molecules and four XerH subunits, where each XerH subunit forms a C-shaped clamp around one arm of difH. The complex exhibits overall two-fold symmetry but differs from other tyrosine recombinases by having a less compact synaptic interface and nearly straight DNA conformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C38 are directly supported by the 2.1 Å resolution crystal structure data presented in Figure 2B and Table 1, with detailed structural observations of protein-DNA interactions shown in Figure 2C and supplementary figures. The structural comparisons with Cre-loxP are well-documented and the DNA binding footprint is validated by DNase I footprinting and mutagenesis experiments.

results.result: XerH exhibits differential binding and cleavage activity at the two arms of difH, with preferential binding to the left arm (KD = 180 nM) over the right arm (KD = 230 nM). This asymmetry is driven by a single base-pair insertion in the left arm and specific interactions between T4 and K290, which dictate distinct protein conformations and define the order of DNA cleavage events.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C59 are well-supported by multiple converging lines of evidence including EMSA binding assays (Figure 3A-B), SEC analysis (Figure 3B), in vitro cleavage assays (Figure 3C-D), in vivo recombination assays in E. coli (Figure 3E), and structural data (Figure 3F-G). The mutagenesis experiments validate the importance of T4 and K290 interactions, and the structural asymmetry is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: The pre-cleavage XerH-difH synaptic complex contains nearly straight DNA with a 165° angle between difH arms, contrasting sharply with the ~100° bend in Cre-loxP complexes. The catalytic tyrosine Y344 is positioned 5.2-5.8 Å from the scissile phosphate in all subunits, indicating a catalytically inactive conformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 are directly supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 3G. The DNA conformation measurements and active site geometry are clearly documented, and the comparison with Cre-loxP is based on well-established structural data. The inactive conformation is consistent with the inability to observe cleavage of intact difH substrates in vitro.

results.result: The post-cleavage XerH-difHLP structure reveals major conformational changes including sharp DNA bending (120° angle) originating from a kink at bases A17'/G18', ~22° rotation of each subunit, and asymmetric activation where subunit A is catalytically active while subunit B remains inactive, consistent with half-of-the-sites reactivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C85 are strongly supported by the 2.4 Å resolution post-cleavage crystal structure (Figure 4A-E, Table 1) and Video 1. The structural changes are well-documented with specific measurements of angles, distances, and interface areas calculated using PISA. The comparison with Cre-loxP structures provides context for the DNA bending mechanism. The use of nicked 'suicide' substrates is appropriate for capturing the post-cleavage state.

results.result: Molecular modeling based on XerH structures predicts that E. coli XerC/D-dif synaptic complexes adopt similar pre- and post-cleavage architectures, with XerD on the left arm and XerC on the right arm. The models predict conformational changes upon FtsK activation consistent with previous smFRET studies showing an increase in dif termini distance from 53 to 67 Å.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C98 are based on homology modeling rather than direct experimental evidence. While the models are informed by high sequence conservation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and are consistent with smFRET data (C97), the assignment of XerC/D to specific arms (C87-C88) is tentative and acknowledged as uncertain by the authors. The predictions require experimental validation.

results.result: Xer recombinases follow the established tyrosine recombinase chemical pathway, but uniquely assemble synaptic complexes in an inactive state with straight DNA that requires major conformational changes for activation. DNA bending occurs post-synaptically rather than concomitantly with complex assembly, providing a regulatory mechanism for faithful chromosome segregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103, C132-C134 represent well-supported conclusions that integrate the structural data from both pre- and post-cleavage complexes with biochemical evidence. The comparison with established tyrosine recombinase mechanisms is appropriate, and the proposed regulatory mechanism is consistent with the known requirement for FtsK activation. These conclusions are directly supported by the experimental data presented.

results.result: The proposed mechanism for XerH recombination begins with cooperative binding of two XerH subunits to difH, with preferential binding to the left arm, followed by tetrameric synaptic complex formation with antiparallel alignment and cyclic domain-swapped arrangement. The pre-cleavage complex contains straight DNA and catalytically inactive XerH.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C113 describe a mechanistic model that is well-supported by the structural data (Figures 2B, 6A-B), EMSA data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and interface calculations from the crystal structures. The cooperative binding and asymmetric configuration are directly demonstrated by experimental evidence. This represents a synthesis of the structural and biochemical findings.

results.result: XerH cannot cleave intact difH substrates in vitro but efficiently cleaves nicked 'suicide' substrates, suggesting that a stimulatory factor (likely FtsK) is required for activation. FtsK may promote conformational rearrangement bringing catalytic tyrosines into active positions and inducing DNA bending, though the exact mechanism requires further investigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C122 combine experimental observations (inability to cleave intact substrates, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) with speculation about FtsK's role. While C114-C116 are supported by data and C118 is supported by citation, C117 and C119-C122 are explicitly speculative. The authors acknowledge uncertainty about FtsK's mechanism (C122), making this result uncertain despite supporting evidence for FtsK requirement.

results.result: Following activation, XerH-catalyzed strand cleavage and rejoining follow the conserved tyrosine recombination pathway with left arm-bound subunits performing first strand exchanges and right arm-bound subunits resolving the Holliday junction.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 are reasonable inferences based on the structural data showing asymmetric activation, the established tyrosine recombinase mechanism (Figure 1B), and the preferential cleavage at the left arm (Figure 3D). While not directly demonstrated for the complete recombination cycle, these claims are well-supported by analogy with other tyrosine recombinases and the structural evidence presented.

results.result: Unlike the paradigm for tyrosine recombinases where DNA bending occurs concomitantly with binding and synapsis, XerH assembles recombination substrates in a straight conformation with DNA bending occurring upon activation by an external factor, providing spatial and temporal regulation of chromosome segregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 are well-supported by the structural data showing straight DNA in the pre-cleavage complex (C127) and bent DNA in the post-cleavage complex. C125-C126 establish the paradigm based on cited literature. C128 is a reasonable inference combining the structural observations with the known requirement for FtsK and its localization to the division septum, though it contains speculative elements about the regulatory mechanism.

results.result: The mechanism of catalytic activation proposed for XerH—preassembly of a synaptic complex with straight DNA followed by FtsK-induced conformational changes—may be conserved in the XerC/D system, as suggested by modeling and consistency with smFRET studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131 extend the XerH findings to XerC/D through modeling (C129) and comparison with smFRET data (C130). While the consistency with smFRET studies provides support, the conservation of the mechanism (C131) remains speculative ('may be conserved') and requires direct experimental validation. The modeling provides a plausible hypothesis but not definitive evidence.

results.result: Chromosome dimers formed by homologous recombination in organisms with circular genomes are resolved by Xer recombinases acting at dif sites located at replication termini. Removal of xer genes or dif sites leads to cell death, and Xer systems can also support plasmid resolution and mobilization of mobile genetic elements.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C9 provide essential background information about Xer recombination and are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature. These claims accurately represent the current understanding of Xer function in bacterial chromosome maintenance and are not contested by the presented data.

results.result: Xer recombinases belong to the tyrosine recombinase superfamily, which catalyzes DNA rearrangements through a conserved mechanism involving tyrosine-mediated strand cleavage, creating 3' phosphotyrosyl linkages and proceeding through Holliday junction intermediates in ordered synaptic complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C16 accurately describe the tyrosine recombinase superfamily and its mechanism based on well-established literature (multiple citations provided). These claims represent accepted knowledge in the field and provide necessary context for understanding the significance of the XerH structures.

results.result: Xer recombination at dif requires the accessory factor FtsK, a DNA motor protein that localizes to the division septum, translocates to replication termini, and activates recombination at Xer-bound dif sites. FtsK regulation ensures Xer recombination occurs only at the appropriate spatial and temporal context.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C22 are well-supported by multiple citations to experimental studies. C22 contains an inference about the regulatory importance of FtsK, but this is a reasonable conclusion based on the cited evidence and the known functions of FtsK and Xer recombination. These claims establish important background for understanding why Xer requires activation.

results.result: The XerH-difH synaptic complex structure differs considerably from other tyrosine recombinases like Cre-loxP, suggesting a model for why Xer proteins require external activation and providing insights into FtsK-mediated stimulation. The structures serve as a resource for modeling other Xer systems including E. coli XerC/D.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by the structural data presented and represent key conclusions of the work. C23 is directly demonstrated by structural comparison (Figure 2B). C24 is a reasonable inference from the structural differences observed. C25 is validated by the successful modeling of XerC/D complexes (Figure 5) and their consistency with smFRET data.

results.result: Mutations of the inner base-pairs of difH arms where XerH makes base-specific contacts abolished or greatly reduced cleavage activity, whereas mutations of neighboring base-pairs did not affect activity.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 is directly supported by cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B. The mutagenesis experiments validate the structural observations of sequence-specific recognition and provide functional confirmation of the protein-DNA interactions observed in the crystal structure.

results.result: The structural data can help improve XerH-based genetic engineering tools for markerless gene deletions in H. pylori.
results.evaluation: Claim C135 is speculative about future applications ('can help') and is supported only by a citation to existing XerH-based tools (Debowski et al., 2012b). While the structural insights may indeed prove useful for tool development, this represents a potential application rather than a demonstrated result of the current work.
